category.name: Cloud Security
category.description: Infrastructure threat modeling: identity, network boundaries, secrets, supply chain and blast radius.

lab.title: CI/CD Deployment Pipeline
lab.summary: A build pipeline that pulls public dependencies, signs nothing, and deploys straight to production.
lab.businessContext: A SaaS team ships several times a day. Their pipeline has grown organically and now holds production credentials, but no one has threat modeled the pipeline itself — only the product it deploys.
lab.systemContext: A push to the Git host triggers a build runner. The runner installs dependencies from a public package registry, reads deployment credentials from a secrets manager, pushes an image to a container registry, and deploys it into the production cluster.

nodes.label: Developer
nodes.description: Pushes commits and opens pull requests

nodes.label: Public Package Registry
nodes.description: Third-party dependency source, resolved at build time

nodes.label: Git Host
nodes.description: Hosts the repository and triggers builds on push

nodes.label: Build Runner
nodes.description: Executes the build, tests and packaging steps

nodes.label: Container Registry
nodes.description: Stores built images consumed by production

nodes.label: Production Cluster
nodes.description: Runs whatever image the pipeline hands it

trustBoundaries.label: Internet
trustBoundaries.description: Untrusted: developers on laptops and the public dependency ecosystem.

trustBoundaries.label: CI / Build
trustBoundaries.description: The build plane. Holds production credentials but is reachable from every commit.

architectureIssues.title: Nothing verifies what production runs
architectureIssues.description: The cluster pulls whatever tag the registry serves. There is no signature or provenance check, so the only thing standing between an attacker and production is write access to the registry.
architectureIssues.hint: If someone replaced the image behind that tag, what in this diagram would notice?

architectureIssues.title: Dependencies resolved from a public registry at build time
architectureIssues.description: Every build reaches out to a third party and executes whatever it gets back, including install scripts, inside a runner holding production credentials.
architectureIssues.hint: The build runs third-party code. What else is in reach of that code?

architectureIssues.title: Production credentials sit in the build plane
architectureIssues.description: The runner can read long-lived deployment credentials on any build, so compromise of any build is compromise of production.
architectureIssues.hint: Which builds actually need to deploy? Do all of them get the same access?

architectureIssues.title: Any push can start a privileged build
architectureIssues.description: The trigger is a push event with no distinction between a trusted branch and an untrusted contribution, so the pipeline treats all code as equally trusted.
architectureIssues.hint: Does a pull request from outside the team run with the same permissions as a merge to main?

architectureIssues.title: Builds share a runner with no isolation stated
architectureIssues.description: Nothing in the design says builds are isolated from each other, so artefacts, caches or credentials from one build may be reachable by the next.
architectureIssues.hint: What is left behind on the runner after a build finishes?

threats.title: Malicious dependency executes inside the build
threats.description: An attacker publishes a package that the resolver picks up — a typo-squat, a compromised maintainer account, or an internal name claimed publicly. Its install script runs on the runner with the runner's full access.
threats.learnerExplanation: A build that installs third-party code is executing third-party code, with everything the build can reach.

threats.title: Deployment credentials stolen from the runner
threats.description: Any code executing during the build — a dependency, a test, a build script — can read the deployment credentials the runner fetched and send them somewhere the attacker controls.
threats.learnerExplanation: Secrets available to the build are available to anything the build runs.

threats.title: Unsigned image swapped before deployment
threats.description: With write access to the registry and no signature verification, an attacker replaces the image behind a tag. Production pulls it and runs it as a normal deployment.
threats.learnerExplanation: Without provenance, "the image in the registry" and "the image we built" are two different claims.

threats.title: Untrusted pull request runs with production access
threats.description: A fork or outside contribution triggers the same privileged pipeline, letting attacker-authored build steps run against the secrets manager.
threats.learnerExplanation: The trigger decides who gets to run code in your build plane.

threats.title: Deployments cannot be attributed afterwards
threats.description: No described record links a running image back to a commit, a build and an approver, so an unauthorised deployment cannot be distinguished from a legitimate one after the fact.
threats.learnerExplanation: If you cannot say which commit is in production, you cannot say whether you have been compromised.

threats.title: One build poisons the next through shared state
threats.description: With no stated isolation, a compromised build writes to a shared dependency cache or workspace, and a later legitimate build picks it up.
threats.learnerExplanation: State that survives a build is state an attacker can leave behind.

threats.title: Pipeline identity can do more than deploy
threats.description: The credential the pipeline uses is scoped to the cluster rather than to a single deployment, so stealing it grants far more than shipping one service.
threats.learnerExplanation: Blast radius is set by what the stolen identity can do, not by how it was stolen.

mitigations.title: Pin dependencies and resolve through an internal mirror
mitigations.description: Commit a lockfile with integrity hashes and resolve through a controlled proxy, so a build cannot silently pull a new or substituted package.

mitigations.title: Short-lived deployment identity via OIDC
mitigations.description: Replace stored long-lived credentials with a token minted per build, scoped to that workflow and expiring in minutes.

mitigations.title: Sign images and verify signatures at admission
mitigations.description: Sign every artefact at build time and have the cluster refuse to run anything without a valid signature from the expected pipeline.

mitigations.title: Separate untrusted-contribution builds from privileged ones
mitigations.description: Run pull-request builds in a workflow with no access to secrets, and require approval before any privileged pipeline runs.

mitigations.title: Ephemeral, isolated runners
mitigations.description: Give every build a fresh runner destroyed afterwards, so nothing persists from one build into the next.

mitigations.title: Record build provenance
mitigations.description: Emit a signed attestation linking image to commit, builder and inputs, and keep it queryable so any running image can be traced back.

mitigations.title: Scope the deploy identity to one workload
mitigations.description: Grant only the permissions needed to update the single service, so a stolen identity cannot take the cluster.

threatMitigations.explanation: Pinned, hash-verified resolution through a controlled mirror is what stops a substituted package entering the build.
A token that expires in minutes and is scoped to one workflow is worth far less to steal than a standing credential.
Verification at admission is what makes a swapped image fail to run rather than deploy normally.
Untrusted code should never run in a workflow that can reach production secrets.
Nothing survives the build, so there is nothing for a compromised build to leave behind.
Signed provenance is what lets you answer "what is actually running, and where did it come from".
Scoping the identity limits what a successful theft actually buys.

releaseGuidance.rationale: Three independent paths — a malicious dependency, a stolen standing credential, or an unsigned image swap — each end in attacker code running in production, and none of them require a privileged position to start. A pipeline in this shape is not a service with some findings against it; it is the control plane for everything the company ships. Holding until signing, short-lived credentials and trigger separation are in place is the defensible call. Arguing for 'ship with conditions' is reasonable if the pipeline is not yet handling real customer traffic and the three critical items are genuinely days away.
suggestedConditions: Replace standing deployment credentials with short-lived, per-build identity before the next production deploy.
Require signature verification at admission so unsigned images cannot run.
Split pull-request builds into a workflow with no access to secrets.
Pin dependencies with integrity hashes and resolve through an internal mirror.
